p.strong: Why the first block has no system in it

div.p: The department fixes the problem, then writes it down. The ticket is a record, not a work order. This is why the form defaults to Closed and why creation can enter any of the three states directly — forcing every ticket through Open would add clicks to record something already finished.
Row lock → legality check → update → audit → outbox → commit → dispatch.

ol.li: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before the transition check. Without the lock, two users acting on one ticket can both read Ongoing, both judge their transition legal, and both write — last writer wins, and the audit log shows a transition that never happened.
The state machine in 07-ticket-state-machine.d2 is enforced in code. The three statuses are not a free-text field the UI happens to constrain.
Audit writes one row per changed field, not one per request. Closing an Ongoing ticket with remarks changes two fields, so it emits two rows.
The outbox row commits with the change — never after, never separately.
The queue job dispatches after commit. Dispatching inside the transaction races the worker: it can pick up the job and query a row that hasn't landed yet.

div.p: Assignment is not in this diagram. assigned_to records who handled the concern; it is a field on the ticket, not a lifecycle stage. Nothing branches on it.
